source: CARE Cambodia (Pailin), "TIP Training on Maize Production" / បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្ដបច្ចេកវិទ្យា ផលិតកម្មដំណំពូតក្របម, 2009. Funded by AusAID (ACIMA project), the European Union (Pailin Food Security Program), and ACIAR (CCPMP project).
text:
Atrazine is one of the two most commonly used weed-killer types for corn production in Cambodia (locally referred to in the Pailin area as "អាសាពន"). Unlike glyphosate and paraquat, atrazine is selective: it kills specific weed types — grasses and some broadleaf weeds — without killing corn.

Timing and method: it is applied before planting, or before weed emergence, targeting grasses and broadleaf weeds that have not yet emerged; it can also be applied after small weeds have emerged, at the early post-emergence stage. Because atrazine is absorbed mainly through the roots of weeds (and of the crop), it should be sprayed to target the soil surface rather than the leaves/stems for best effectiveness — spraying onto weed foliage is less effective.

Toxicity: medium toxicity. Its residue can remain active in the soil for several months. The source notes that atrazine is banned for use in European Union countries, because residues of this chemical have been found contaminating groundwater and streams.

Caution: the source specifically warns that atrazine is strongly damaging to rice, and that spray equipment or containers used with atrazine must not be rinsed into clean/fresh water sources.
